---
title: "Uplift Modeling"
description: "A modeling approach that estimates how an intervention changes an outcome for different individuals or groups."
term: "Uplift Modeling"
letter: "U"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

Uplift modeling estimates who is more likely to change behavior because
of an intervention, such as a discount or reminder. It focuses on the
difference the intervention makes, rather than only predicting who is
likely to act.

## Technical explanation

Uplift modeling estimates heterogeneous treatment effects using treatment
and control data. A common target is conditional average treatment effect,
$\tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]$, where $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ are potential
outcomes under treatment and control. Individual-level causal effects
cannot both be observed for the same unit, so estimation requires
assumptions and appropriate experimental design.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

It can help allocate interventions to people who benefit, avoid spending
resources on those who would act anyway, and reduce interventions that
cause harm. Valid conclusions depend on randomization or defensible
causal assumptions, not predictive accuracy alone.

## How it works

Collect outcomes from treated and control groups, estimate treatment
effects as a function of features, and rank or segment cases by expected
uplift. Evaluate with randomized holdout data and causal metrics, while
checking treatment cost, harms, and subgroup effects.

Randomized assignment supports estimating average treatment effects;
estimating which individuals benefit requires additional modeling and
validation.

## Practical example

A retailer can randomize eligible customers to receive or not receive a
coupon, then estimate which customer segments show incremental purchases.
Test the policy on a separate randomized holdout before deploying it.

## Common misconceptions

- A response-propensity model predicts who is likely to act; uplift
  estimates how the intervention changes behavior.
- Correlation in observational data is not enough to identify a causal
  treatment effect without assumptions and adjustment.
